steps: No. A scientific theory is not an ultimate truth.
It is an explanation supported by available observations and experimental evidence.
New evidence may require the theory to be modified or replaced.
items.finalAnswer: A scientific theory is well-supported but not an ultimate, unchangeable truth.

steps: Yes. Laws of nature are based on observations and experiments made with the knowledge and tools available at the time.
If new evidence does not agree with a law, scientists may revise or extend it.
A law may remain useful within the limits in which it has been tested.
items.finalAnswer: Existing laws may be revised in the light of new evidence.

steps: A doctor uses scientific knowledge to diagnose diseases and choose suitable treatments.
An engineer uses scientific knowledge to design and construct buildings, machines and other structures.
A farmer uses scientific knowledge to improve crops by selecting suitable seeds, fertilizers and methods of cultivation.
items.finalAnswer: Doctors, engineers and farmers use scientific knowledge in their work.

steps: A theory is accepted as long as its predictions agree with observations and experimental results.
If reliable new observations or experiments contradict its predictions, the theory needs to be modified or rejected.
A theory may also be replaced by another theory that explains the evidence better.
items.finalAnswer: A theory is modified or rejected when reliable evidence contradicts its predictions.

steps: A scientific theory must be testable.
It must be possible to imagine an observation or experiment that could show the theory to be wrong.
A theory that can only be supported, but cannot possibly be disproved by testing, is not a scientific theory.
items.finalAnswer: A scientific theory must be capable of being tested and potentially disproved.

steps: New ideas that challenge established truths are often met with doubt and resistance.
People may be reluctant to give up ideas that have been accepted for a long time.
A new idea is generally accepted when repeated observations and experiments provide strong evidence for it.
items.finalAnswer: New ideas are often resisted at first and accepted when supported by strong evidence.

steps: No. An untestable hypothesis is not necessarily wrong.
It cannot be checked by observations or experiments, so science cannot establish whether it is right or wrong.
A hypothesis must be testable to be examined scientifically.
items.finalAnswer: An untestable hypothesis cannot be judged scientifically as right or wrong.

steps: A small amount of data may support a prediction, but it cannot prove that the prediction will always be correct.
For example, observing many white swans does not prove that all swans are white.
However, one reliable observation of a swan that is not white is enough to show that the prediction “all swans are white” is not always correct.
items.finalAnswer: Many confirming observations cannot prove a universal prediction, but one counterexample can disprove it.
